item.title: Wall Street steadies following jarring drops for AI stocks worldwide
item.description: A sell-off for artificial-intelligence stocks is hitting Wall Street again Thursday after whipping around the world on worries about how much longer the AI frenzy will last.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — Wall Street is steadying Thursday following jarring drops for stocks worldwide in the artificial intelligence industry on worries about how much longer the AI frenzy will last. After initially falling to a loss following its worst day since July, the S&P 500 quickly erased it and added 0.2 per cent to edge closer to its all-time high set last week. Continued weakness for AI stocks dragged the Nasdaq composite down 0.2 per cent. But most of the rest of the U.S. stock market nevertheless rose, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 470 points, or 0.9 per cent, as of 1:19 p.m. Eastern time. Markets were much shakier earlier in the day. A sell-off for AI stocks that began on Wall Street Wednesday whipped around the world and sent South Korea’s Kospi stock index down 7.6 per cent and Japan’s Nikkei 225 down 4.9 per cent. They’re the latest swings for AI stocks after they led the market for years. Companies are pouring money into the technology in hopes of bigger profits and improved productivity. But data centers and AI chips cost money, and many companies have been borrowing the cash to get them. Now, after yields in bond markets worldwide hit their highest levels in years and made borrowing money more expensive, worries are rising about how resilient that boom in spending can be. Many AI-related companies have already taken on debt to build out their aspirations, and stocks are struggling under the debt loads. CoreWeave, which offers AI computing power to customers over the cloud, slipped early in trading before moving 1.4 per cent higher. It tumbled 15.5 per cent a day earlier. It said in the summer that it had US$4.41 billion in principal payments to make on its debt over the second half of this year and another US$6.18 billion in 2027. It had more than US$5.5 billion in cash, as of June 30. High yields in the bond market also generally make investors less willing to pay high prices for stocks, particularly those seen as the most expensive. Nvidia, the chip company that’s ridden the AI boom to become Wall Street’s most valuable company, fell 1.6 per cent and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. It came into the day with a nearly 1,415 per cent gain since the end of 2022. The losses for AI stocks moderated as the day progressed, which helped broad U.S. indexes to steady. CoreWeave had been down as much as 9.5 per cent in the morning before erasing the loss and gaining ground, while stocks outside of AI were much more resilient. Marsh & McLennan helped lead the market after the insurance and professional services firm reported a stronger profit for the summer than analysts expected. The company, which updated its brand name to Marsh earlier this year, also made more revenue than expected, and its stock climbed 5.5 per cent. Expectations are high for profits at all kinds of companies this reporting season, which began in earnest this week. That’s what’s allowed U.S. stocks to set records despite high inflation and many other worries weighing on Wall Street. Now, companies will need to surpass those high expectations to drive their stock prices even higher. Seven out of every 10 stocks within the S&P 500 rose. But because AI stocks have become so big in value, their stock movements have more effect on the index and can drown out the rest of the market. In the bond market, Treasury yields fell, which means investors were willing to pay higher prices to buy U.S. government bonds. Treasurys have a reputation as a safer investment, one with less risk of the borrower going bankrupt, and investors often flock to them when feeling nervous. The yield on the 10-year Treasury sank to 5.09 per cent from 5.19 per cent late Wednesday. It had topped 5.30 per cent earlier this month and touched its highest level since 2002 because of worries about high inflation, signals of a strong U.S. economy and other factors. The drop in yields came even though another report signaled inflation has worsened in the United States by more than economists expected. Several reports on the U.S. economy also came in stronger than economists expected, which typically pushes yields upward. One report said U.S. retailers made more money last month than economists expected, while another said fewer U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week than expected. In stock markets abroad, South Korea’s loss was the headliner. Its Kospi index is dominated by two chip companies, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, and it fell to its worst day since July. It has dropped 39 per cent since setting a record in June. Indexes were stronger in Europe, which has less of a dependence on tech stocks, and London’s FTSE 100 rallied 1.1 per cent for one of the world’s biggest gains. ___ Stan Choe, The Associated Press AP Business Writers Chan Ho-him and Matt Ott contributed to this report.

item.title: AI firm Cohere to buy cybersecurity company Aisle
item.description: Canadian artificial intelligence firm Cohere says it has signed a letter of intent to purchase a cybersecurity business.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Canadian artificial intelligence firm Cohere says it has signed a letter of intent to purchase a cybersecurity business. Cohere’s acquisition target is Aisle, a company split between San Francisco and Prague that has developed AI systems capable of uncovering and remediating vulnerabilities in software. Cohere did not immediately reveal the value or structure of the deal, as well as its expected closing date. Cohere framed the proposed transaction as a way to further develop sovereign AI and invest in Europe, the home of its recent acquisitions Aleph Alpha and Reliant AI. Aisle was started last year by Ondrej Vlcek, the ex-chief executive of Avast, a Czech antivirus provider. Vlcek and his two fellow co-founders will take on leadership roles at Cohere, which has promised to make a substantial long-term investment in Prague to further expand Aisle. --- Tara Deschamps, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2025.

item.title: Competition Bureau says Quebec real estate board violated abuse of dominance rules
item.description: The Competition Bureau says it has reached a settlement with Quebec’s real estate industry association to loosen restrictions that violated the Competition Act.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: The Competition Bureau says it has reached a settlement with Quebec’s real estate industry association to loosen data-sharing restrictions that violated the Competition Act. The watchdog says the Quebec Professional Association of Real Estate Brokers and its subsidiary, Société Centris, broke abuse of dominance rules by refusing to provide its members with a real estate data feed, while also restricting how such data could be used. The bureau says lack of access to that data was likely meant to “impede innovation and limit competition in the real estate brokerage services market.” As part of a consent agreement reached with the association, it will now provide its members with a real estate data feed containing information about sale prices, listing history and property characteristics. Pierre-Olivier Simard, president of the QPAREB board of directors, says in a statement that the solution is “tailored to the Quebec reality,” given that Quebec’s laws are more restrictive than those in the rest of Canada when it comes to the protection of personal information. The bureau launched its investigation into QPAREB’s data-sharing practices in 2023 after a previous case against the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board, in which the watchdog challenged rules that prevented brokers in that region from sharing certain real estate data with their clients through secure online platforms. --- Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026.

item.title: Selling the losers in your stock portfolio can help save you tax
item.description: Nobody likes taking a loss when selling stocks, but experts say now is the time to look at your portfolio and see if there are any investments that haven’t worked out as you hoped that might help you ...
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA — Nobody likes taking a loss when selling stocks, but experts say now is the time to look at your portfolio and see if there are any investments that haven’t worked out as you hoped that might help you reduce your tax bill. Reviewing your portfolio and taking a look at what gains you’ve seen and how you might be able to offset them with any losses should be part of your year-end tax planning. Kris Kibler, tax planning lead at Wealthsimple, says if you are selling shares at a loss, that deficit can be used to offset capital gains on better performing stocks, reducing the amount of tax you will owe. He explained that if you bought shares for $10,000 and later sold them for $7,000, the $3,000 capital loss could be deducted against capital gains. That deduction will reduce the amount of tax you might owe when you file your return next year. Kibler says it is important that tax-loss selling isn’t done in a vacuum. “You don’t necessarily engage in tax-loss harvesting or tax-loss selling in order to just take advantage of the tax implication with disregard for the investment portfolio overall,” he says. “This always wants to be kind of done in tandem with your overall investment and financial plan as a whole.” It is also important to ensure you don’t run afoul of the rules governing what losses you can claim. Tax-loss selling only applies to taxable or non-registered accounts. Losses in accounts such as your TFSA, RRSP or RESP cannot be used to offset your taxable gains outside those accounts. The losses can only be used to offset any taxable capital gains you have. They can’t be deducted from your regular income. If you don’t have any capital gains to offset this year, your losses can be used to reduce your taxable capital gains going back three years or you can carry the losses forward to use in future years. CRA also doesn’t allow what is referred to as a superficial loss, which prevents you from claiming the loss if the same or identical security is repurchased within a 61-day window starting 30 calendar days before the sale and extending 30 days after the sale. The superficial loss rules don’t just apply to your account, but also extend to your spouse or common-law partner, corporations you or your spouse control, or what the CRA calls an affiliated person. “What the CRA doesn’t want you to do is get the advantages of the tax-loss harvesting or tax-loss selling strategy in order to get the benefit and then purchase the exact same securities again and continue in the same portfolio,” Kibler said. Julie Petrera, director of financial planning at Edward Jones, says it is important to remember that tax-loss selling is not an investment strategy. “It should support your long-term goals but not drive your long-term investing goal,” she said. “I wouldn’t make decisions on what I’m holding in my portfolio just for short-term tax reasons.” Petrera said losses are part of investing at times, but tax-loss selling is the “silver lining” when you have securities that have gone down. “While you have lost money on that security or on that investment, the money that you’ve lost could be made up for in tax savings applied to another investment,” she said. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 15, 2026. Craig Wong, The Canadian Press
